unpackings.studentFriendly: I can analyze how grammar, usage, and mechanics shape meaning and credibility, and I can apply the conventions of Standard English deliberately when creating and revising texts.
know: Standard English conventions provide shared expectations for formal written communication.
Grammar describes how words, phrases, and clauses function together.
Usage involves selecting forms and constructions appropriate to a communication situation.
Mechanics includes capitalization, punctuation, and other written conventions.
Grammatical choices can affect clarity, emphasis, tone, rhythm, and interpretation.
Writers can deliberately vary sentence structures while maintaining grammatical control.
Punctuation can clarify relationships among ideas and create rhetorical effects.
Formal academic writing and other communication contexts may call for different registers.
Editing improves accuracy, but effective revision also considers meaning and audience.
Language variation is not evidence of intellectual ability; writers make choices according to purpose, audience, and context.
understand: Conventions support clear communication and establish expectations within particular settings.
Grammar and mechanics are tools for constructing meaning rather than isolated rules.
Experienced writers evaluate the effects of language choices as well as their correctness.
Control of conventions supports credibility in academic and professional contexts.
Writers can distinguish purposeful stylistic variation from unintentional errors.
Effective editing requires understanding the intended meaning of a sentence.
do: Analyze the grammatical structures of complex sentences.
Evaluate how usage and mechanics influence clarity and rhetorical effect.
Identify and correct errors that obscure meaning or undermine formal communication.
Apply appropriate punctuation and capitalization in original writing.
Maintain consistent and purposeful grammatical relationships.
Revise sentences for clarity, concision, emphasis, and coherence.
Evaluate the effectiveness of conventional and stylistically unconventional constructions.
Edit academic, literary, and professional texts according to audience and purpose.
Explain the rationale for significant editing decisions.

vocabulary.definition: The system of structures and patterns governing how language is formed.
vocabulary.example: Examining how a dependent clause relates to an independent clause.

vocabulary.definition: The selection and application of language forms appropriate to a context.
vocabulary.example: Choosing a formal register for a research paper.

vocabulary.definition: Written conventions such as punctuation and capitalization.
vocabulary.example: Using a colon to introduce an explanation.

vocabulary.definition: A variety or level of language suited to a particular situation.
vocabulary.example: Using different language in a college application essay and a text message.

vocabulary.definition: A clause containing a subject and predicate that can stand alone as a sentence.
vocabulary.example: The researchers published their findings.

vocabulary.definition: A clause that cannot function as a complete sentence by itself.
vocabulary.example: Although the results were unexpected.

vocabulary.definition: The use of corresponding grammatical forms to express related ideas.
vocabulary.example: The project required planning, researching, and revising.

vocabulary.definition: A word, phrase, or clause that describes or limits another element.
vocabulary.example: The carefully documented findings persuaded the committee.

vocabulary.definition: A punctuation mark that can connect closely related independent clauses or separate complex list items.
vocabulary.example: The evidence was persuasive; the committee approved the proposal.

vocabulary.definition: A punctuation mark used after an independent clause to introduce an explanation, example, or list.
vocabulary.example: The committee reached one conclusion: further research was necessary.

vocabulary.definition: Expressing ideas efficiently without sacrificing essential meaning.
vocabulary.example: Replacing 'due to the fact that' with 'because.'

vocabulary.definition: The influence a language choice has on an audience.
vocabulary.example: A brief sentence emphasizing a conclusion.

targets: I can analyze how grammar influences meaning.
I can apply Standard English conventions in formal writing.
I can use punctuation to clarify relationships among ideas.
I can revise sentences for clarity and rhetorical effect.
I can distinguish intentional stylistic choices from unintentional errors.
I can explain and justify my editing decisions.

suggestedTexts.title: Letter from Birmingham Jail
suggestedTexts.author: Martin Luther King Jr.
suggestedTexts.purpose: Analyze sentence structure, punctuation, and grammatical parallelism in a sophisticated argument.
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Provide historical context and annotate complex sentence structures.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: Sentence construction reinforces the urgency and logic of an argument.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: How does the arrangement of clauses shape emphasis and persuasion?

suggestedTexts.title: The Story of an Hour
suggestedTexts.author: Kate Chopin
suggestedTexts.purpose: Examine how grammatical and punctuation choices support pacing, perspective, and ambiguity.
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Provide historical context and discuss themes of death and marriage.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: Subtle sentence choices influence a story's surprising interpretation.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Which sentence-level choices contribute to the story's final effect?

suggestedTexts.title: The House on Mango Street
suggestedTexts.author: Sandra Cisneros
suggestedTexts.purpose: Compare purposeful stylistic sentence choices with conventions used in formal academic prose.
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Select short passages and provide discussion of narrative voice.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: A writer's distinctive voice can challenge expectations about conventional sentence structure.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: What would be lost if every sentence were rewritten in formal academic style?

suggestedTexts.title: A Student Research Draft and Edited Version
suggestedTexts.author: Teacher-created or permission-cleared student examples
suggestedTexts.purpose: Evaluate how editing decisions improve precision, coherence, and credibility.
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Provide side-by-side versions and highlight selected changes.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: Small sentence-level revisions can make a complicated argument much easier to follow.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Which edits change meaning, and which primarily change presentation?

differentiation.title: Find the Sentence Boundaries
differentiation.activity: Students identify independent and dependent clauses, repair fragments and run-ons, and explain how punctuation clarifies relationships.
scaffolds: Color-code clauses and model several repairs.
differentiation.success: Students correctly revise four sentences and explain two decisions.

differentiation.title: Edit for Meaning
differentiation.activity: Students compare unclear and revised sentences, identify the source of confusion, and make targeted edits.
scaffolds: Provide a checklist for agreement, modifiers, punctuation, and clarity.
differentiation.success: Students improve five sentences without changing the intended meaning.

differentiation.title: The Sentence Revision Laboratory
differentiation.activity: Students revise a paragraph three ways to emphasize different ideas, varying clause structure, punctuation, and sentence length.
scaffolds: Model the rhetorical effects of two contrasting revisions.
differentiation.success: Students produce three purposeful versions and explain their effects.

differentiation.title: The Editorial Conference
differentiation.activity: Pairs edit a formal argumentative paragraph for grammatical accuracy, clarity, consistency, and rhetorical effectiveness.
scaffolds: Require explanations for substantive changes.
differentiation.success: Students submit an improved paragraph with a justified revision record.

differentiation.title: Grammar as Rhetorical Design
differentiation.activity: Students analyze sentence-level choices in two accomplished writers, imitate selected techniques in original prose, and annotate how their constructions influence audience interpretation.
scaffolds: Distinguish stylistic imitation from copying content.
differentiation.success: Students demonstrate grammatical control and sophisticated explanation of rhetorical effects.

questions.prompt: Which revision most effectively corrects the sentence 'The evidence was compelling, the committee approved the recommendation'?
options: The evidence was compelling; the committee approved the recommendation.
The evidence was compelling the committee approved the recommendation.
The evidence, was compelling the committee, approved the recommendation.
The evidence was compelling, and, the committee approved the recommendation.
questions.answer: The evidence was compelling; the committee approved the recommendation.
questions.rationale: A semicolon appropriately joins two closely related independent clauses.

questions.prompt: Which sentence demonstrates parallel structure?
options: The researcher was careful, persistent, and worked accurately.
The researcher valued accuracy, persistence, and clarity.
The researcher valued accuracy, being persistent, and to communicate clearly.
The researcher was accurate, with persistence, and communicating clearly.
questions.answer: The researcher valued accuracy, persistence, and clarity.
questions.rationale: The coordinated items use corresponding grammatical forms.

questions.prompt: Revise a complex but unclear sentence from a draft. Explain how your changes improve clarity without altering its meaning.
questions.answer: A strong response includes a grammatically sound revision and explains the effect of specific changes.
questions.rationale: Students demonstrate purposeful editing rather than mechanical correction alone.

questions.prompt: Explain why a deliberate sentence fragment in a literary work may be effective even though it would be inappropriate in some formal academic contexts.
questions.answer: A strong response distinguishes intentional stylistic effect from the conventions expected in different communication situations.
questions.rationale: Students evaluate language choices in relation to genre, audience, and purpose.

questions.prompt: Revise a 250-word analytical paragraph for grammatical accuracy, effective mechanics, clarity, and rhetorical emphasis. Annotate five significant decisions and explain their effects.
questions.answer: Evaluate grammatical control, clarity, purposeful sentence choices, and accuracy of explanations.
questions.rationale: The task integrates analysis, evaluation, and construction.

evidence: Annotated analysis of sentence structures and punctuation.
Edited paragraphs demonstrating control of formal conventions.
Before-and-after revisions with explanations.
Original writing using deliberate grammatical and rhetorical choices.
An editing reflection identifying recurring patterns and improvements.
instruction: Teach grammar and mechanics through authentic texts and student writing.
Model the connection between conventions, meaning, and rhetorical effect.
Use sentence combining and revision rather than isolated correction alone.
Distinguish formal Standard English expectations from the legitimacy of language variation.
Provide focused editing conferences and opportunities to apply feedback.
Evaluate purposeful stylistic choices within their genres and contexts.
watchFor: Treating every unconventional literary construction as an error.
Correcting surface features without checking intended meaning.
Teaching punctuation as disconnected memorized rules.
Confusing grammatical complexity with effective writing.
Overediting student voice.
Assuming formal academic conventions apply identically to every genre.

unpackings.studentFriendly: I can compare perspectives across texts, investigate the visible and hidden influences shaping them, evaluate how an author's experiences and circumstances affect their choices, and synthesize credible research into an informed understanding.
know: Authors and speakers communicate perspectives shaped by experience, knowledge, discipline, and circumstances.
Different texts may frame the same topic in ways that shape audience perceptions or beliefs.
Perspective can be established through claims, examples, omissions, language, imagery, and structure.
Texts may be influenced by commercial relationships, sponsorships, advertising, ownership, and financial incentives.
Commercial influence may not be immediately visible to the audience.
Historical and disciplinary contexts can shape stylistic and thematic decisions.
An author's personal perspective may interact with professional expectations and institutional pressures.
Credible research requires evaluating authorship, expertise, evidence, currency, and potential conflicts of interest.
Synthesis combines information from multiple sources to develop a coherent understanding.
Responsible analysis distinguishes demonstrated influences from unsupported speculation.
understand: Perspective shapes how information is selected, developed, and interpreted.
A single topic can be represented through several defensible or competing perspectives.
The circumstances of text creation may influence its content and style.
Commercial incentives can shape communication even when a text appears informational.
A writer's perspective should be evaluated through evidence rather than assumed from identity alone.
Credible synthesis involves comparing, reconciling, and integrating sources rather than merely summarizing them separately.
Understanding influence helps readers become more critical and independent interpreters.
do: Compare and contrast perspectives across several texts addressing a common topic.
Analyze how authors establish and develop their perspectives.
Explain how language, evidence, organization, and omissions may shape audience beliefs.
Investigate sponsorship, ownership, advertising, affiliate relationships, and other commercial influences.
Distinguish disclosed financial relationships from less-visible incentives.
Evaluate the influence of historical, disciplinary, and personal perspectives on thematic and stylistic choices.
Research a complex question using credible sources representing relevant perspectives.
Evaluate source reliability and conflicts of interest.
Synthesize evidence into an original explanation or argument.
Cite sources appropriately and acknowledge uncertainty.

vocabulary.definition: A way of interpreting or presenting a subject shaped by knowledge, experience, and circumstances.
vocabulary.example: A scientist and a community resident emphasizing different aspects of a proposed project.

vocabulary.definition: The selection and presentation of information to encourage a particular understanding.
vocabulary.example: Describing a policy primarily through its cost or its potential benefits.

vocabulary.definition: The effect of financial interests or business relationships on a text.
vocabulary.example: A product review published through an affiliate marketing arrangement.

vocabulary.definition: Material funded or supported by an advertiser or sponsor.
vocabulary.example: An article labeled as a paid partnership.

vocabulary.definition: Advertising designed to resemble the surrounding editorial content.
vocabulary.example: A paid promotional feature formatted like a magazine article.

vocabulary.definition: A relationship or incentive that could compromise or appear to compromise impartial judgment.
vocabulary.example: A reviewer receiving compensation from a company whose product is reviewed.

vocabulary.definition: An approach shaped by the methods and assumptions of a field of study.
vocabulary.example: An economist and an environmental scientist examining the same development.

vocabulary.definition: An interpretation shaped by the circumstances and knowledge of a particular time.
vocabulary.example: A nineteenth-century author's treatment of industrial labor.

vocabulary.definition: A decision about the ideas or concerns emphasized in a text.
vocabulary.example: Focusing a novel on the tension between individual freedom and social expectations.

vocabulary.definition: A decision involving language, form, organization, or presentation.
vocabulary.example: Using restrained scientific language instead of an emotional appeal.

vocabulary.definition: The degree to which a source is trustworthy and appropriately supported.
vocabulary.example: A research report that identifies methods and provides verifiable evidence.

vocabulary.definition: The integration of ideas and evidence from multiple sources into a coherent understanding.
vocabulary.example: Combining historical records, scientific findings, and community testimony to explain an issue.

targets: I can compare how different authors frame a common topic.
I can explain how perspectives influence audience perceptions.
I can identify visible and less-visible commercial influences.
I can evaluate how historical, disciplinary, and personal perspectives shape texts.
I can distinguish credible evidence from unsupported assumptions.
I can synthesize several credible sources into a coherent explanation.
I can document sources and acknowledge competing interpretations.

suggestedTexts.title: The Danger of a Single Story
suggestedTexts.author: Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie
suggestedTexts.purpose: Examine how narrative selection and perspective shape beliefs about people and cultures.
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Provide captions and context for cultural references.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: The stories people encounter can influence how they understand entire communities.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: How does the speaker demonstrate that perspective is constructed through selective storytelling?

suggestedTexts.title: The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks
suggestedTexts.author: Rebecca Skloot
suggestedTexts.purpose: Compare scientific, historical, ethical, and personal perspectives on medical research.
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Provide historical and scientific context; review sensitive material.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: The same medical discovery can be understood differently by researchers and affected families.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: How do disciplinary and personal perspectives shape what different participants consider important?

suggestedTexts.title: Silent Spring
suggestedTexts.author: Rachel Carson
suggestedTexts.purpose: Analyze how scientific expertise, historical circumstances, and rhetorical choices shape a public argument.
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Provide context for mid-twentieth-century environmental debates.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: Scientific writing can challenge powerful economic interests.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: How do scientific evidence and historical context influence the author's thematic and stylistic choices?

suggestedTexts.title: A Sponsored Article and an Independent Report
suggestedTexts.author: Teacher-selected publishers
suggestedTexts.purpose: Investigate commercial incentives, disclosure practices, framing, and credibility.
suggestedTexts.access: Verified publisher websites or school databases.
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Provide screenshots or accessible copies showing relevant disclosures.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: A polished article may have financial relationships readers need to understand.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: What evidence establishes a commercial relationship, and how might it influence the text?

suggestedTexts.title: A Research Source Set on Artificial Intelligence in Education
suggestedTexts.author: Teacher-curated researchers, educators, and organizations
suggestedTexts.genre: Research articles, policy reports, journalism, and commentary
suggestedTexts.purpose: Compare disciplinary and institutional perspectives and synthesize credible evidence.
suggestedTexts.access: Academic databases, official reports, and verified publications.
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Provide a mix of concise summaries and appropriately challenging full texts.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: Different stakeholders make competing claims about the same emerging technology.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: How do expertise, institutional interests, and evidence shape each source's conclusions?

differentiation.title: Two Perspectives, One Topic
differentiation.activity: Students read two short texts about the same issue, identify each central claim, and compare the evidence and language used.
scaffolds: Provide claim-identification prompts and sentence stems.
differentiation.success: Students identify two similarities or differences and support them with examples.

differentiation.title: Follow the Funding
differentiation.activity: Students examine examples of sponsored content, independent reporting, and affiliate-linked reviews to identify disclosed relationships and possible incentives.
scaffolds: Model how to locate publisher information and advertising disclosures.
differentiation.success: Students identify the nature of two commercial relationships and explain their possible relevance.

differentiation.title: The Perspective Matrix
differentiation.activity: Students compare three texts addressing one issue, documenting claims, evidence, audience, framing, historical context, and authorial perspective.
scaffolds: Require a specific quotation or paraphrase for each analytical claim.
differentiation.success: Students explain how differing perspectives produce distinct representations of the issue.

differentiation.title: Who Influenced This Text?
differentiation.activity: Students investigate the authorship, publisher, funding, disclosures, and evidence behind a public-facing article, then write a source evaluation.
scaffolds: Distinguish verified financial relationships from hypothetical concerns.
differentiation.success: Students produce an evidence-supported evaluation without making unsupported accusations.

differentiation.title: Synthesize, Don't Stack
differentiation.activity: Students investigate a focused research question using four credible sources and write a synthesis organized around themes or findings rather than source-by-source summaries.
scaffolds: Model synthesis paragraphs that connect and qualify sources.
differentiation.success: Students develop a coherent answer supported by appropriately cited evidence from multiple sources.

differentiation.title: The Influence Investigation
differentiation.activity: Students investigate a consequential public issue by comparing scientific, commercial, journalistic, and personal perspectives. They examine documented institutional incentives and create an annotated synthesis explaining how these influences shape public understanding.
scaffolds: Require transparent sourcing, consideration of counterevidence, and explicit uncertainty statements.
differentiation.success: The final analysis integrates credible research and carefully distinguishes documented influences from inference.

questions.prompt: Two articles discuss the same proposed environmental policy. One emphasizes business costs, while the other emphasizes health benefits. What is the strongest initial inference?
options: Both articles must contain false information
The authors may frame the issue through different perspectives and priorities
The articles necessarily have identical audiences
Neither article can be evaluated
questions.answer: The authors may frame the issue through different perspectives and priorities
questions.rationale: Differences in emphasis can reveal contrasting perspectives without proving dishonesty.

questions.prompt: Which finding provides the clearest evidence of a commercial influence on a product review?
options: The reviewer uses descriptive language
The reviewer discusses an expensive product
The reviewer discloses receiving a commission from purchases made through links
The review includes a photograph
questions.answer: The reviewer discloses receiving a commission from purchases made through links
questions.rationale: A disclosed affiliate relationship establishes a financial incentive relevant to evaluating the review.

questions.prompt: Explain how historical circumstances and professional expertise might lead two authors to make different stylistic and thematic choices about the same topic.
questions.answer: A strong response identifies relevant circumstances, describes specific choices, and explains the connections using evidence.
questions.rationale: Students evaluate how historical and disciplinary perspectives influence texts.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes a synthesis paragraph from a sequence of unrelated source summaries?
questions.answer: A synthesis develops a shared idea by comparing, connecting, qualifying, or reconciling information from multiple credible sources.
questions.rationale: Students demonstrate understanding of research-based synthesis.

questions.prompt: Investigate a complex topic using at least four credible sources representing different perspectives. Analyze how the texts establish perspective, identify any documented commercial or institutional influences, evaluate contextual effects on style and theme, and synthesize findings into an original evidence-based report.
questions.answer: Evaluate comparative analysis, evidence of influence, contextual reasoning, source credibility, integration of findings, and citation accuracy.
questions.rationale: The task integrates all four Authors & Speakers expectations.

evidence: A comparative analysis of perspectives across texts.
An investigation of disclosed or documented commercial influences.
An analysis of historical, disciplinary, and personal influences on craft.
A credible source evaluation matrix.
An original synthesis supported by multiple cited sources.
instruction: Teach perspective through comparative reading rather than isolated identification of bias.
Use real examples of sponsored content and financial disclosures.
Distinguish commercial influence from automatic proof of inaccuracy.
Model how to investigate authorship, ownership, sponsorship, and expertise.
Require textual evidence for claims about stylistic and thematic choices.
Teach synthesis as integration of findings, not a collection of summaries.
Include academic databases and credible primary sources.
Emphasize ethical citation and careful treatment of uncertainty.
watchFor: Assuming every difference in perspective indicates misinformation.
Treating an author's identity as sufficient proof of a particular viewpoint.
Accusing a source of hidden influence without evidence.
Confusing sponsored content with all forms of advertising.
Equating commercial funding with automatic falsehood.
Summarizing sources separately without synthesizing their findings.
Using numerous sources without evaluating credibility.
Ignoring evidence that complicates an initial conclusion.

11.T.C.2.a.studentFriendly: I can compare how different texts develop perspectives and influence readers' beliefs.
know: Perspective is developed through evidence, framing, language, and emphasis.
understand: Different representations of the same issue can shape audience perceptions.
targets: I can explain how two or more texts construct different perspectives.
instruction: Use paired and multi-source comparative reading.
evidence: An evidence-based comparative analysis.
watchFor: Comparing conclusions without analyzing how perspectives are developed.

11.T.C.2.b.focus: Identify influencers, including less-visible commercial influences
11.T.C.2.b.studentFriendly: I can investigate who or what influences a text, including financial interests that may not be obvious.
know: Ownership, sponsorship, advertising, and financial relationships can influence texts.
understand: Recognizing documented incentives supports critical evaluation.
targets: I can explain a documented influence without making unsupported claims.
instruction: Analyze authentic disclosure and sponsorship examples.
evidence: A documented influence analysis.
watchFor: Assuming an undisclosed relationship exists without evidence.

11.T.C.2.c.focus: Evaluate historical, disciplinary, and personal influences
11.T.C.2.c.studentFriendly: I can explain how an author's circumstances and expertise influence themes and style.
know: Historical conditions, professional disciplines, and personal experiences can shape authorial choices.
understand: Context can influence what authors emphasize and how they communicate.
targets: I can connect contextual evidence with specific authorial choices.
instruction: Pair close reading with focused contextual research.
evidence: A contextual analysis supported by textual examples.
watchFor: Reducing a complex text to assumptions about the author's background.

11.T.C.2.d.studentFriendly: I can combine credible research to answer complex academic or personal questions.
know: Credible research involves evaluating sources and integrating findings.
understand: Synthesis creates a coherent understanding that draws from multiple sources.
targets: I can develop an original, evidence-based synthesis.
instruction: Use evidence matrices and thematic synthesis models.
evidence: A properly sourced synthesis report.
watchFor: Writing disconnected summaries instead of integrating ideas.

unpackings.studentFriendly: I can evaluate how arguments use evidence, reasoning, rhetorical techniques, and logical fallacies to influence audiences, and I can strategically combine these techniques to construct convincing, responsible arguments.
know: Arguments communicate claims supported by reasons and evidence.
Argumentative techniques include claims, counterclaims, rebuttals, concessions, evidence, and rhetorical appeals.
Argumentative texts can combine logical, ethical, and emotional appeals.
Rhetorical techniques influence how audiences interpret arguments and respond to claims.
Logical fallacies are errors in reasoning that weaken the relationship between evidence and conclusions.
Common fallacies include false dilemma, hasty generalization, straw man, ad hominem, circular reasoning, and false cause.
Arguments can use accurate evidence but still employ flawed reasoning.
Writers make choices about evidence, organization, and language according to audience and purpose.
Rhetorical devices such as parallelism, repetition, analogy, and rhetorical questions can strengthen an argument.
Ethical argumentation requires accurate representation of evidence and opposing perspectives.
understand: An argument's effectiveness depends on its reasoning, evidence, rhetorical choices, and intended audience.
Persuasive impact and logical soundness are related but not identical.
Logical fallacies can distort audience understanding even when they initially seem convincing.
Multiple rhetorical appeals can reinforce one another when integrated purposefully.
Counterarguments and concessions can strengthen credibility.
Analyzing an argument requires evaluating how techniques contribute to meaning rather than simply identifying them.
Responsible writers consider the consequences of their rhetorical choices.
do: Read, discuss, evaluate, and critique argumentative texts across genres and modes.
Identify claims, reasons, evidence, counterclaims, and rebuttals.
Evaluate how argumentative techniques contribute to meaning and central ideas.
Identify and explain logical fallacies in written, spoken, and multimodal texts.
Distinguish persuasive language from well-supported reasoning.
Select and apply argumentative techniques suited to audience and purpose.
Integrate multiple rhetorical devices or appeals strategically.
Address counterarguments fairly and respond with evidence.
Revise arguments to improve logic, clarity, credibility, and audience engagement.

vocabulary.definition: An arguable position that a writer or speaker seeks to establish.
vocabulary.example: Schools should provide more opportunities for independent reading.

vocabulary.definition: A position that challenges or complicates an argument's main claim.
vocabulary.example: Additional reading time might reduce time for other activities.

vocabulary.definition: A reasoned response to an opposing claim.
vocabulary.example: Explaining how a proposed schedule accommodates both concerns.

vocabulary.definition: Acknowledgment that an opposing position has some merit.
vocabulary.example: Recognizing that implementation would require resources.

vocabulary.definition: A rhetorical appeal relying on reasons, evidence, or logical relationships.
vocabulary.example: Using reliable data to support a recommendation.

vocabulary.definition: A rhetorical appeal based on credibility, character, or demonstrated expertise.
vocabulary.example: A scientist explaining relevant qualifications and methods.

vocabulary.definition: A rhetorical appeal engaging an audience's emotions or values.
vocabulary.example: A personal account illustrating the human effects of a policy.

vocabulary.definition: An error in reasoning that undermines an argument.
vocabulary.example: Assuming that two events occurring together proves one caused the other.

vocabulary.definition: A fallacy that misrepresents an opposing argument to make it easier to attack.
vocabulary.example: Claiming that someone who supports shorter homework assignments opposes learning.

vocabulary.definition: A fallacy presenting only two alternatives when other possibilities exist.
vocabulary.example: Either eliminate technology or abandon meaningful instruction.

vocabulary.definition: A conclusion drawn from insufficient or unrepresentative evidence.
vocabulary.example: Judging an entire program based on one participant's experience.

vocabulary.definition: A fallacy attacking a person instead of addressing the person's argument.
vocabulary.example: Rejecting a proposal solely because the speaker is inexperienced.

vocabulary.definition: A fallacy assuming a causal relationship without adequate support.
vocabulary.example: Concluding that a new schedule caused higher test scores simply because both occurred together.

vocabulary.definition: The repetition of corresponding grammatical structures for emphasis or clarity.
vocabulary.example: We must investigate carefully, evaluate fairly, and act responsibly.

vocabulary.definition: A question asked primarily to encourage reflection or emphasize a point.
vocabulary.example: What kind of community do we want to build?

targets: I can evaluate the effectiveness of argumentative techniques.
I can explain how arguments influence meaning and audience response.
I can identify and analyze logical fallacies.
I can support claims with credible evidence and reasoning.
I can respond fairly to counterarguments.
I can integrate multiple rhetorical appeals and devices purposefully.
I can revise an argument to improve its effectiveness and integrity.

differentiation.title: Find the Argument
differentiation.activity: Students color-code claims, reasons, evidence, and counterclaims in a short editorial and explain how the components work together.

differentiation.success: Students accurately identify major components and explain the argument's central idea.

differentiation.title: Fallacy Detective

differentiation.title: The Argument Audit
differentiation.activity: Students evaluate an editorial for evidence quality, reasoning, counterarguments, and rhetorical appeals, then write a critique supported by quotations.
scaffolds: Provide criteria for distinguishing persuasive impact from logical soundness.
differentiation.success: Students produce an evidence-based evaluation identifying strengths and weaknesses.

differentiation.title: Build a Responsible Argument
differentiation.activity: Students develop a claim about a school or community issue, research evidence, address a counterclaim, and incorporate at least two rhetorical appeals.
scaffolds: Model concession and rebuttal paragraphs.
differentiation.success: The final argument combines sound reasoning, credible evidence, and purposeful appeals.

differentiation.title: The Rhetoric and Reasoning Lab
differentiation.activity: Students compare two sophisticated arguments on a contested issue, identify rhetorical strengths and logical weaknesses, and compose a nuanced original response that integrates multiple appeals without relying on fallacies.
scaffolds: Require fair representation of opposing positions and documented evidence.
differentiation.success: Students demonstrate nuanced evaluation and strategically integrated rhetorical techniques.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes a logical fallacy?
options: A claim supported by credible evidence
An error in reasoning that weakens an argument
Any argument containing emotion
A conclusion that challenges popular opinion
questions.answer: An error in reasoning that weakens an argument
questions.rationale: A fallacy concerns defective reasoning rather than whether an argument is emotional or unpopular.

questions.prompt: A speaker argues, 'Either we eliminate all homework or we do not care about students.' Which fallacy is most evident?
options: False dilemma
Valid deduction
Concession
Analogy
questions.answer: False dilemma
questions.rationale: The statement presents only two alternatives while excluding reasonable possibilities.

questions.prompt: Select a paragraph from an argument and evaluate how its evidence and rhetorical techniques contribute to its central idea.
questions.answer: A strong response identifies techniques, cites evidence, and explains their effects rather than simply naming them.
questions.rationale: Students evaluate argumentative construction and implications for meaning.

questions.prompt: Explain how a writer could combine logos, ethos, and pathos in an argument about improving public transportation.
questions.answer: A strong response proposes credible evidence, trustworthy expertise, and a relevant human perspective without substituting emotion for reasoning.
questions.rationale: Students demonstrate strategic integration of rhetorical appeals.

questions.prompt: Write an evidence-based argument for an authentic audience. Include a clear claim, credible evidence, a fair counterargument, a rebuttal, and at least two strategically integrated rhetorical devices or appeals. Annotate your choices and evaluate the reasoning for fallacies.
questions.answer: Evaluate argumentative effectiveness, logical soundness, evidence, fair treatment of opposing views, and rhetorical integration.
questions.rationale: The task assesses all four expectations.

evidence: An annotated analysis of argumentative techniques.
A logical fallacy identification and explanation exercise.
A critique of an argument's reasoning and rhetorical effectiveness.
An original evidence-based argument incorporating multiple appeals.
A reflection explaining how rhetorical choices serve audience and purpose.
instruction: Teach claims, evidence, and reasoning before introducing complex rhetorical analysis.
Distinguish logical validity from emotional persuasiveness.
Use authentic examples of flawed and effective arguments.
Model analysis of how rhetorical techniques shape meaning.
Teach fair counterargument and responsible rebuttal.
Require students to explain the intended effect of each rhetorical device.
Evaluate ethical reasoning alongside persuasive effectiveness.
watchFor: Identifying an appeal without explaining its function.
Labeling every emotional argument fallacious.
Assuming a persuasive argument must be logically sound.
Using fallacy labels without explaining the actual reasoning error.
Misrepresenting counterarguments.
Treating rhetorical devices as decorative additions.
Substituting confident language for credible evidence.

11.T.T.3.a.studentFriendly: I can critique how argumentative techniques influence meaning and audience response.
know: Arguments use evidence, reasoning, organization, and rhetorical choices.
understand: Argumentative techniques influence interpretation and effectiveness.
targets: I can explain how a technique supports or weakens an argument.
instruction: Use annotated mentor arguments and evidence-based critiques.
evidence: An argumentative technique analysis.
watchFor: Naming a technique without analyzing its effect.

11.T.T.3.b.studentFriendly: I can identify flawed reasoning and explain how it affects an argument.
know: Logical fallacies weaken the relationship between reasons and conclusions.
understand: Flawed reasoning can mislead audiences.
targets: I can explain why an argument contains a specific reasoning error.
instruction: Compare flawed and revised arguments.
evidence: A fallacy analysis with explanations.
watchFor: Treating disagreement as evidence of a fallacy.

11.T.T.3.c.studentFriendly: I can choose techniques that strengthen my argument for a particular audience.
know: Argumentative choices should support purpose and audience engagement.
understand: Strategic argumentation combines sound reasoning with effective communication.
targets: I can construct a credible and engaging argument.
instruction: Use authentic argumentative writing and revision.
evidence: An original argument with justified choices.
watchFor: Choosing persuasion over accuracy.

11.T.T.3.d.focus: Integrate multiple rhetorical devices or appeals
11.T.T.3.d.studentFriendly: I can combine rhetorical techniques to strengthen my message.
know: Appeals and rhetorical devices can reinforce one another.
understand: Effective integration depends on audience, context, and purpose.
targets: I can integrate multiple rhetorical techniques purposefully.
instruction: Analyze combinations of appeals in mentor texts.
evidence: A rhetorically developed argument with annotations.
watchFor: Adding devices mechanically without considering their effects.

unpackings.status: draft — independently developed instructional guidance; educator review recommended
unpackings.studentFriendly: I can manage a flexible writing process by setting a purpose, considering my audience, researching and organizing ideas, drafting with intention, evaluating feedback, revising for effectiveness, and editing for accuracy.
know: Writing is a recursive process rather than a fixed sequence of steps.
Writers establish goals based on purpose, audience, and context.
Modes, genres, and organizational structures offer different ways to communicate.
Prior knowledge, research, and discussion support idea generation.
Planning involves selecting and prioritizing relevant information.
Drafting requires purposeful decisions about ideas, diction, syntax, and craft.
Evaluation considers whether a text achieves its intended purpose.
Feedback can reveal gaps in clarity, evidence, organization, and audience awareness.
Revision involves substantive changes to meaning, structure, and rhetorical effectiveness.
Editing addresses conventions, consistency, and surface-level accuracy.
Writers may return to earlier stages as new information or insights emerge.
understand: Effective writers adapt their processes to different tasks, audiences, and purposes.
Clear goals provide criteria for evaluating a draft.
Planning should remain flexible as understanding develops.
Strong writing requires deliberate selection and organization of ideas.
A first draft is a working version rather than a finished product.
Feedback is most useful when interpreted in relation to the writer's goals.
Revision and editing address different aspects of writing quality.
An effective writing process balances creativity, critical evaluation, and accuracy.
do: Establish a purpose, writing goals, and target audience.
Select appropriate modes, genres, structures, and organizational approaches.
Generate ideas using prior knowledge, research, and discussion.
Evaluate and prioritize information according to relevance and impact.
Develop an initial draft using appropriate language, sentences, and craft techniques.
Evaluate a draft through self-review and external feedback.
Revise ideas, organization, information, diction, and craft for effectiveness.
Edit for grammar, usage, punctuation, and other written conventions.
Document and explain significant decisions across the writing process.
Move flexibly among planning, drafting, researching, evaluating, and revising.

vocabulary.definition: The flexible set of activities writers use to develop and improve texts.
vocabulary.example: Returning to research after discovering a gap in a draft.

vocabulary.definition: The intended outcome or effect of a text.
vocabulary.example: Explaining a problem or persuading an audience to act.

vocabulary.definition: The specific readers, listeners, or viewers a text is designed to reach.
vocabulary.example: Local decision-makers considering a proposal.

vocabulary.definition: A form through which communication is delivered.
vocabulary.example: Written prose, audio, visuals, or multimodal presentation.

vocabulary.definition: A recognizable type of text with particular conventions.
vocabulary.example: Editorial, memoir, research report, or feature article.

vocabulary.definition: The arrangement of information and ideas within a text.
vocabulary.example: Problem-solution or comparison-contrast organization.

vocabulary.definition: The development of potential content through thinking, research, and discussion.
vocabulary.example: Brainstorming questions before beginning a research essay.

vocabulary.definition: The degree to which information contributes to a particular purpose.
vocabulary.example: Selecting evidence that directly supports a central claim.

vocabulary.definition: Developing an initial or intermediate version of a text.
vocabulary.example: Writing an exploratory introduction before refining the thesis.

vocabulary.definition: Assessing one's own work against goals and criteria.
vocabulary.example: Checking whether a conclusion addresses the intended audience.

vocabulary.definition: Information from other writers or readers that can guide improvement.
vocabulary.example: A peer identifying a gap in an explanation.

vocabulary.definition: Reconsidering and changing a text to improve its meaning or effectiveness.
vocabulary.example: Reorganizing paragraphs to strengthen an argument.

vocabulary.definition: Correcting or refining a text's language conventions and consistency.
vocabulary.example: Correcting agreement, punctuation, and capitalization.

vocabulary.definition: A process in which earlier stages are revisited as work develops.
vocabulary.example: Returning to planning after receiving feedback on a draft.

vocabulary.definition: A deliberate language or structural choice used to create an effect.
vocabulary.example: Using a brief anecdote to introduce a complex issue.

targets: I can identify my purpose, goals, and intended audience.
I can choose a suitable genre, mode, and organization.
I can generate ideas through research, reflection, and discussion.
I can prioritize relevant and impactful information.
I can draft using purposeful language and craft.
I can evaluate whether my draft achieves its goals.
I can revise substantially in response to feedback.
I can edit my work for accuracy and conventions.
I can explain how my writing changed throughout the process.

suggestedTexts.title: The House on Mango Street
suggestedTexts.author: Sandra Cisneros
suggestedTexts.purpose: Study how a writer's selection, organization, and language choices support a distinctive narrative purpose.
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Use short vignettes and provide guided craft analysis.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: A concise piece of writing can communicate a complex experience.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: How might the author have selected and revised details to achieve this effect?

suggestedTexts.title: The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks
suggestedTexts.author: Rebecca Skloot
suggestedTexts.purpose: Examine how research, organization, and narrative craft support complex nonfiction.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: Research and storytelling work together to make a complicated issue understandable.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: How does the author organize researched information for a broad audience?

suggestedTexts.title: The Danger of a Single Story
suggestedTexts.author: Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie
suggestedTexts.purpose: Analyze purposeful organization, audience awareness, and the selection of illustrative experiences.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: Carefully arranged stories build toward a broader argument.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: What choices would a writer need to plan and refine to produce this structure?

suggestedTexts.title: A Published Essay and Its Revision History
suggestedTexts.author: Teacher-selected author or permission-cleared student writer
suggestedTexts.purpose: Investigate how planning, feedback, revision, and editing change a text.
suggestedTexts.access: Teacher-created materials, published author drafts, or permission-cleared student work.
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Provide annotated versions with changes highlighted.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: A finished essay may look dramatically different from its first draft.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Which revisions changed the ideas, and which corrected presentation?

suggestedTexts.title: A Public Information Guide
suggestedTexts.author: Teacher-selected credible organization
suggestedTexts.purpose: Evaluate how genre, design, information selection, and editing meet audience needs.
suggestedTexts.access: Credible public websites or teacher-created examples.
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Select an accessible guide with clear headings and readable structure.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: The effectiveness of practical writing depends on the reader being able to use it.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: How would this guide change if the audience were unfamiliar with the topic?

differentiation.title: Start with Purpose
differentiation.activity: Students identify a writing task's purpose and audience, then select a suitable genre and organizational structure.
scaffolds: Provide sample audience profiles and genre examples.
differentiation.success: Students develop a clear purpose statement and explain their organizational choice.

differentiation.title: From Ideas to Outline
differentiation.activity: Students brainstorm ideas, review a short source, discuss possibilities with a partner, and organize relevant details into an outline.
scaffolds: Model how to distinguish central ideas from less relevant details.
differentiation.success: Students produce an outline with a clear focus and logically grouped support.

differentiation.title: Revise or Edit?
differentiation.activity: Students compare two drafts and categorize changes as revision or editing, then apply both types to a short paragraph.
scaffolds: Model changes to organization separately from corrections to conventions.
differentiation.success: Students make and explain two substantive revisions and three editing corrections.

differentiation.title: Draft with Intention
differentiation.activity: Students plan and draft a researched explanatory or argumentative text for a defined audience, documenting choices about evidence, organization, diction, and craft.
scaffolds: Provide a model demonstrating how an outline can evolve during drafting.
differentiation.success: Students produce a coherent draft and explain several purposeful craft choices.

differentiation.title: The Revision Conference
differentiation.activity: Students exchange drafts, provide feedback linked to the writer's purpose, revise major weaknesses, and complete a separate editing pass.
scaffolds: Use specific feedback questions about audience, evidence, and organization.
differentiation.success: Students document meaningful revisions and produce a conventionally edited final draft.

differentiation.title: The Editorial Production Studio
differentiation.activity: Students develop a publication-ready essay or feature for an authentic audience, using research, multiple drafts, editorial conferences, substantive revision, and a documented editing process.
scaffolds: Require an audience analysis, editorial rationale, and revision history.
differentiation.success: The final publication demonstrates a flexible, reflective writing process and clear rhetorical effectiveness.

questions.prompt: What should most directly guide a writer's initial choices about genre and organization?
options: The writer's favorite font
The purpose, goals, and target audience
The length of the first paragraph
The number of available images
questions.answer: The purpose, goals, and target audience
questions.rationale: These factors establish the communication needs that planning should address.

questions.prompt: A student has gathered extensive research but cannot organize a draft. What is the most productive next step?
options: Include every source in the order it was found
Identify the most relevant information and connect it to an organization plan
Begin editing punctuation before drafting
Discard all research and start over
questions.answer: Identify the most relevant information and connect it to an organization plan
questions.rationale: Purposeful selection and organization connect research with writing goals.

questions.prompt: Explain how audience awareness should influence diction, sentence structure, and craft techniques during drafting.
questions.answer: A strong response proposes specific choices suited to an identified audience and explains their effects.
questions.rationale: Students connect drafting decisions with rhetorical purpose.

questions.prompt: Which change is primarily a substantive revision rather than an edit?
options: Correcting a misspelled word
Adding a missing comma
Reorganizing paragraphs to strengthen the argument
Correcting subject-verb agreement
questions.answer: Reorganizing paragraphs to strengthen the argument
questions.rationale: Substantive revision improves the text's ideas or effectiveness, while editing addresses conventions.

questions.prompt: A peer says your draft contains useful information but does not clearly address its intended audience. Describe how you would evaluate and revise the draft.
questions.answer: A strong response uses the writing goals to evaluate the draft and proposes specific changes to information, organization, language, or craft.
questions.rationale: Students apply feedback through purposeful evaluation and revision.

questions.prompt: Produce a complete writing-process portfolio for a text intended for an authentic audience. Include a purpose statement, audience analysis, planning materials, research notes, initial draft, feedback, revised draft, edited final version, and a reflection explaining significant decisions.
questions.answer: Evaluate purpose and audience alignment, planning, idea development, drafting, feedback use, substantive revision, editing, and process reflection.
questions.rationale: The task integrates all eight Writing Processes expectations.

evidence: A writing purpose statement and target-audience profile.
A plan identifying mode, genre, and organization.
Idea-generation notes and research records.
An outline connecting relevant information with writing goals.
An initial draft demonstrating purposeful craft choices.
Self-evaluation and external feedback.
A revised draft with documented substantive changes.
An edited final text and process reflection.
instruction: Model writing as a flexible and recursive process.
Use authentic audiences and meaningful writing purposes.
Teach students to select modes, genres, and structures deliberately.
Provide structured opportunities for research, discussion, and planning.
Demonstrate how writers prioritize information.
Use mentor texts to analyze effective drafting choices.
Teach self-evaluation and feedback as separate but complementary processes.
Distinguish substantive revision from editing.
Assess process decisions as well as final products.
watchFor: Treating writing as a rigid sequence that cannot be revisited.
Planning without a clear purpose or audience.
Including all gathered information regardless of relevance.
Mistaking a complete first draft for a finished text.
Giving feedback limited to grammar and punctuation.
Revising only individual words when the structure is ineffective.
Editing before addressing major problems in meaning.
Accepting feedback mechanically without evaluating it against writing goals.

11.P.EICC.4.a.studentFriendly: I can identify why I am writing, what I want to accomplish, and whom I want to reach.
know: Purpose, goals, and audience guide writing decisions.
understand: Clear intentions establish criteria for effectiveness.
targets: I can establish a clear rhetorical situation for my writing.
instruction: Use authentic writing scenarios and audience profiles.
evidence: A purpose statement and audience analysis.
watchFor: Beginning without considering intended readers.

11.P.EICC.4.b.studentFriendly: I can choose the format and structure that best fit my writing purpose.
know: Different modes, genres, and structures serve different communication needs.
understand: Organizational choices influence accessibility and impact.
targets: I can justify my organizational plan.
instruction: Compare organizational models and mentor texts.
evidence: A writing plan with a rationale.
watchFor: Choosing a structure only because it is familiar.

11.P.EICC.4.c.focus: Generate ideas through knowledge, research, and discussion
11.P.EICC.4.c.studentFriendly: I can develop writing ideas using what I know, what I research, and what I discuss with others.
know: Idea generation draws on multiple sources of information.
understand: Research and discussion can expand and refine ideas.
targets: I can develop relevant ideas using several approaches.
instruction: Use inquiry questions, brainstorming, and source gathering.
evidence: Idea-generation notes and research records.
watchFor: Relying exclusively on initial assumptions.

11.P.EICC.4.d.studentFriendly: I can organize ideas and highlight the information that will matter most to my readers.
know: Information varies in relevance, usefulness, and impact.
understand: Effective selection strengthens coherence and purpose.
targets: I can justify why particular information belongs in my text.
instruction: Use evidence sorting and reverse outlining.
evidence: A prioritized outline or evidence map.
watchFor: Including information simply because it was collected.

11.P.EICC.4.e.studentFriendly: I can combine ideas, language, and craft techniques to produce a draft that serves my audience.
know: Drafting integrates content, diction, syntax, and craft.
understand: Purposeful language choices influence audience engagement.
targets: I can draft a coherent text with purposeful choices.
instruction: Use mentor texts and guided drafting conferences.
evidence: An initial draft with annotations.
watchFor: Prioritizing polished sentences over developing ideas.

11.P.EICC.4.f.focus: Evaluate effectiveness through review and feedback
11.P.EICC.4.f.studentFriendly: I can evaluate whether my draft achieves its goals and use feedback to identify improvements.
know: Evaluation compares a draft against purpose and writing goals.
understand: Self-review and external feedback reveal different opportunities for improvement.
targets: I can identify strengths and specific priorities for revision.
instruction: Use focused feedback rubrics and writer conferences.
evidence: A self-evaluation and feedback record.
watchFor: Treating every suggestion as equally relevant.

11.P.EICC.4.g.studentFriendly: I can make meaningful changes to improve my ideas, organization, information, language, and craft.
know: Revision addresses the substance and effectiveness of a text.
understand: Major improvements may require rethinking earlier choices.
targets: I can explain how revisions improve the text.
instruction: Use revision plans and comparison of drafts.
evidence: A substantially revised draft and rationale.
watchFor: Limiting revision to proofreading.

11.P.EICC.4.h.studentFriendly: I can edit my writing to meet appropriate conventions and communicate accurately.
know: Editing addresses grammar, usage, punctuation, and consistency.
understand: Conventions support clarity and credibility.
targets: I can produce a carefully edited final text.
instruction: Use targeted editing passes and convention checklists.
evidence: An edited final version.
watchFor: Editing without first completing necessary substantive revision.
